The tree’s versatile look and approachable price point also helped it overtake the Best Choice Products Pencil Christmas Tree for our ‘Best Slim Tree’ pick. “The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly,” says Tubbs.

We always research products thoroughly before including them, and test every single one. Our reviews are thorough, in-depth, and honest. We put ourselves in the shoes of the shopper (because most of the time, we are the ones shopping!), and make sure that we’re answering the questions that we would want answered in the buying process.

We favored natural-looking trees that are easy to set up. We also took shipping into account and tested trees that arrive not only in style, but with speed.

All trees that were reviewed were unboxed, set up (and lit up) by our contributors. They lived with trees and experienced all they had to offer firsthand, so that they could share the real deal with our readers.

What Size Christmas Tree Is Right for Me?

First and foremost, the height of your fake Christmas tree should depend on the height of your ceiling. A good rule of thumb is to keep your tree at least one-and-a-half feet lower than your ceiling, otherwise, it will look crowded. “I like to leave about six to12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in,” says Shea McGee (more on the designer’s holiday advice below). Both McGee and Jeff Leatham, the floral designer who helped mastermind Kendall Jenner’s festive holiday house, agree that seven to eight feet hits a sweet spot in most homes. “The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe,” says McGee.

Some people want to avoid the hassle (and extra cost) of buying a fresh tree each year, while others are allergic to real trees or are concerned about the fire safety hazard that comes along with real trees (they can become highly flammable as they dry out). Others (including people with pets) know that a real Christmas tree can be bait for disaster. Fresh or faux is really a matter of personal preference, and anyone who wants a fake Christmas tree should go for it. Leatham points out that in faux trees, the branches don’t drop, the coloring stays vibrant, and there’s often more structure to add extra ornaments.

Is It Better to Get a Pre-Lit Tree Or to Do It Yourself?

Choosing if you want your tree pre-lit is one of the first decisions you’ll make when navigating the vast artificial tree world. Pre-lit options are the preference of holiday decor gurus like Leatham. “Always, always, always go for prelit—it makes the tree look more full and realistic,” he tells us. Our editors like that pre-lit Christmas trees are convenient to set up (opposed to blindly garlanding string lights) and how they help guarantee your lighting scheme will look uniform. That said, drawbacks include potentially difficult repairs. While you can easily unstring removable lights to troubleshoot, built-in LEDs might pose bigger technical issues. On the other hand, stringing your own lights may be a more complex, time-consuming process, but you’ll ultimately have more control over which areas of your tree are spotlighted.

How Should You Decorate Your Christmas Tree?

You’ve gotten your tree up, fluffed the branches, and poured yourself a nice cup of hot cocoa or eggnog to celebrate—now comes the fun part: decorating. While there’s no right way to decorate your Christmas tree, we looked through our archives for some tips and tricks to give your setup some extra sparkle.

If your mentality is “more is more,” your holiday hero will be Kathy Hilton, who greeted AD back in 2021 with four artificial Christmas trees decked out with all the bells and whistles (emphasis on the bells). One tip we’d steal from Hilton is the idea that the decorations don’t have to go up all at once. “I normally start decorating in October, then keep adding until December,” says Hilton.

Kendall Jenner, on the other hand, favors a more traditional tree, dipped in nostalgic classics like tinsel, twinkle lights, and vintage Christopher Radko ornaments that were passed down by her mother, Kris. Her designer reveals that she even loves stringing popcorn for the tree and dried orange slices on garlands. “Every year, more and more of my clients want more traditional holiday decorations that they can invest in, collect, and pass on to other generations,” says Leatham. “I love that idea of seeing the same ornaments every year and having them bring back wonderful memories.” Since we have a feeling you have your own collection of heirloom Christmas decorations that have been collecting dust, we’d look to the supermodel for inspiration.

Color scheming your ornament display is one way to set yourself apart from the pack. “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” says Annie Sloan, color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. Stylist Dorcia Kelley of Kelle Miles Studio also suggests using a planter instead of a traditional tree stand or skirt for a modern look. “When hanging ornaments, you want to make sure you’re hanging it towards the end of the branch instead of right at the tip. This way, they’ll be more stable,” she says.

We also recommend playing with shapes, textures, and finishes to create as much interest as possible. AD’s perfect Christmas tree (pictured at the top of this article) features lots of vintage-inspired John Derian ornaments that bring on the kitsch, accented with classic ball ornaments in a range of sizes to create depth and dimension. A color palette of muted blue and bold metallic hues complement the deep green branches while slivers of silver tinsel add holiday pizzazz.

Fluffing your artificial Christmas tree is the key to convincingly faking the real thing. Most of the time, your tree will arrive with all the branches up-turned straight out of the box, and you’ll first want to mount the tree in its stand or collar. Next comes the actual fluffing—as reviewer Pujah Shah mentioned, it’s a smart idea to wear some work gloves to avoid any pricking that might occur while you’re working through the branches. Starting at the bottom, you’ll fan the largest branches down, layer by layer, until you reach the very top (where the branches become much shorter). If your branches have smaller tips built in, we like the center-right-left method of starting toward the base of the tree and positioning the smaller tips first center, next towards the right, and lastly towards the left, until you’ve reached the end. After that, you’ll go branch by branch, noticing that your tree looks full and much more lush with each adjustment. Afterwards, all that’s left to do is make any minor fixes to eliminate bald spots and voila!

What’s the Best Real Christmas Tree to Buy?

Again, that’s completely a matter of personal preference. Trees come in a variety of hues, some with a dark green, some with a blue tint, and others with a bright shade. Some have spiky needles while others are soft to the touch. Trees vary by geographical region and what's native to your area, but some of the most popular options used as Christmas trees across the U.S. include the Fraser Fir, Balsam Fir, Douglas Fir, and Blue Spruce (all of which are available in faux varieties, as well!).

How Does the Lifetime Cost of a Faux Tree Compare to Annually Buying a Real Tree?

While how much your real Christmas tree costs will vary depending on its size as well as where you live in the United States, expect to spend anywhere from $40 to well over $100. In a few years, that running total will start to cost you, but with an artificial tree, you’ll pay the total cost up front. High-quality trees can also last you up to 15 years, making the sometimes extravagant price tags more digestible, especially in the later years when you’re no longer burdened with figuring out the logistics of strapping that netted Douglas Fir onto the car roof.

Flocking refers to the process of dusting your artificial Christmas tree with a powdery white overcoat to mimic the appearance of fresh snowfall. Some trees—like the Yaheetech tree Brie Schwartz tested—come pre-flocked, but if you prefer a DIY moment, ready-to-flock sprays are also available at most big box retailers. We like Balsam Hill’s guide to flocking your tree, which details a recipe for homemade flocking, as well as all the safety precautions you’ll want to take: Like wearing protective gear, flocking in a well-ventilated environment, and ensuring you’re using non-hazardous materials. (Though if your budget allows, we think it might be best to invest in one of the brand’s ready-flocked trees.)

In the grand scheme of artificial Christmas trees, King of Christmas and Balsam Hill are widely known as the crème de la crème, thanks to their realistic appearance, convenient setup, and thoughtful extras like complimentary storage bags for the off-season. While both fall into the category of more luxuriously-priced holiday decor, Balsam Hill’s price points are slightly higher ($349 to $4,000+ while King of Christmas ranges from $229 to $3,000+).

In our own quests for the most elite faux trees, we’ve also tried both brands. Commerce vice president Divya Viswanathan called Balsam Hill’s Fraser Fir “the Christmas tree of my dreams,” while contributor Andrea Lewis previously called her Blue Spruce from the brand “a lovely addition to our holiday traditions—elegant, easy to manage, and captures that cozy, Christmas air perfectly.” AD’s global director of audience development Pujah Shah became a King of Christmas convert last holiday after testing the brand’s Alpine Fir tree. “I wanted something tall, sleek, and a little bit dramatic that felt intentional in a modern space but still cozy enough for family chaos—it nails both,” says Shah. We think that both brands are great options—it’s hard to beat how realistic Balsam Hills designs are, and holiday floral designer and one of our experts, Jeff Leatham even named King of Christmas as his favorite brand. To choose the right brand for you, we recommend figuring out what will suit your space and your decorations, as well as establishing a price point you’re comfortable with.

We tapped the designer and creative force behind one of our favorite interior brands, McGee & Co., on the best ways to make your artificial Christmas tree really pop this season. Read on for her advice on how to make merry with a beautiful, yet intentional holiday set up.

Is There Such a Thing as an Ideal Sized Christmas Tree?

“When you’re choosing a tree, the ideal size really depends on your space. I like to leave about 6–12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in. For most standard spaces, a 7-7.5-foot tree hits the sweet spot. If you have tall ceilings, you can absolutely go bigger—9-12 feet fills the volume beautifully. And in smaller rooms, a slimmer silhouette keeps things festive without overwhelming the layout. The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe.”

What are Some of the Design Benefits of Choosing an Artificial Christmas Tree Versus a Real One?

“I love the flexibility an artificial tree gives you. You know exactly what shape and fullness you’re getting, and the branches stay right where you want them—which makes decorating so much easier and more polished. They also hold up all season long, which is great if you like to decorate early. And of course, you can reuse them year after year, which means you can invest in the style you love and bring it back every holiday.”

How Do You Make an Artificial Christmas Tree Look More Realistic?

“Start with a tree that already has a natural, realistic base—good branch texture goes a long way. From there, keep your palette cohesive so the whole tree feels curated instead of busy. I love layering garlands because they add that organic movement you see in real trees. Then finish with meaningful ornaments, ribbon, and a few organic touches—like dried citrus or pinecones. Those add warmth and authenticity, making even a faux tree feel beautifully lifelike.”

“Both options have their place. A pre-lit tree is all about ease—the lights are perfectly placed, and you get that warm glow the minute you plug it in. It’s great if you want a beautiful tree without the extra steps. An unlit tree gives you more creative freedom. You can layer different styles of lights, change the mood from year to year, and really customize the look. It takes a bit more time, but it can feel incredibly intentional. So, if you want quick and polished, go pre-lit. If you love the process of styling every detail, unlit is the way to go.”

The easiest way to make your artificial Christmas tree look like a real tree is to, well, cover it up. Go heavier on the decorations this year: Think garland, Christmas lights, pinecones, ornaments, a tree topper, etc. We're talking the works. Check out our go-to holiday decor tips that will make the best Christmas trees look even more magical.

It’s affordable in bulk, doubles as a garland, and covers quite a bit of real estate from low to high. And who doesn’t love a bow? We pulled an option to satisfy the minimalists as well as some embellished trim that’s got major maximalist appeal.

A dead giveaway—no pun intended—that your tree’s a fake is the base: that plastic, mechanical-esque tree stand. Cover that metal stand up with a festive tree skirt (or basket!) as you would with real Christmas trees.

If your tree doesn’t have pre-strung lights, head to the holiday aisle for some white or multicolored lights. Some of our favorites include unconventional and more delicate-looking lights that don’t necessarily scream “Christmas.” They’ll draw the eye to the center of the tree and take the attention off of the branches. Besides, you can never have too many lights in your home decor during the holiday season.

When scouting out ornaments for your tree, look for options with serious heirloom potential. Kendall Jenner’s Christopher Radko’s classic ornament collection is a good example—and Etsy sellers have troves of vintage ornaments to start your own traditions or recreate the supermodel’s holiday style. These miniature bulbs we found at Terrain are a fun way to create more depth when paired with larger balls, and we like that the different colors really pop when your tree is lit. We also turned to John Derian for gorgeous, traditional options pictured on our tree.

#4872. Ethereum Sets December 15 Date for Delayed Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade

Ethereum Sets December 15 Date for Delayed Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade

Ethereum developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi test network for December 15, 2026, more than a month after security concerns forced them to call off the fork.

The upgrade will activate on Hoodi at 19:12 UTC that day, at epoch 143,616, developers agreed during an All Core Devs Consensus (ACDC) call on Thursday, according to an AI-generated summary of the meeting and notes from tracker EIPsInsight. They chose December 15 over December 16.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Client teams on both the execution and consensus layers are expected to cut releases for the fork by early next week.

The upgrade has already gone live on Sepolia, another Ethereum test network, where it began producing blocks in October with a gas limit more than three times mainnet's. Developers have not yet set a date for mainnet.

The Hoodi fork was originally due on October 26, but developers postponed it after security firm ChainSecurity warned that Glamsterdam's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existingsmart contracts, citing 13 real-world examples.

At the center of the concerns is EIP-8037, which raises the cost of creating new data on Ethereum to slow the growth of the network's state, the data every node must store, as block gas limits rise. It also meters that cost separately from other computation, which allows gas to be returned to a contract during execution, something some existing contracts' security checks do not expect.

After reviewing feedback from execution layer clients, developers reached rough consensus on Thursday to ship EIP-8037 as is, rather than delay the upgrade further or change the specification, though some participants raised concerns about potential breakage and the usefulness of the GAS opcode, which reports how much gas remains in a transaction.

Under the proposal, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as it does today, and deploying a 24 kB contract about eight times as much. Its authors said the change would cap state growth at a target of about 120 GiB a year at a 150 million gas limit.

Consensus layer teams also agreed on a fix for how they validate blocks from builders, picking a less disruptive option that most teams considered a stopgap over a cleaner solution that would have required a consensus-breaking change.

Developers did not decide whether to keep FOCIL, a proposal designed to make it harder for block builders to censor transactions, as a headline feature of Hegotá, Ethereum's next upgrade after Glamsterdam.

Some participants argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, while others said both could be developed in parallel. FOCIL keeps its status as a headline feature until the next ACDC call, around December 10, when developers expect to decide Hegotá's full scope.

Developers agreed to give post-quantum and AI security threats higher priority, at what the summary described as a "DEFCON 2-3" level of urgency. The Ethereum Foundation has said AI posed a more urgent threat to the network than quantum computing.

#4868. 5 Best Hotel Sheets for a Boutique Bedscape (2026)

We want to let you in on a secret: You can replicate the good night’s rest you get at luxury destinations by dressing your bed with the hotel-quality sheets. Aside from accessories like fluffy down feather pillows and mattress toppers, we often attribute cotton percale and sateen to a five-star sleep.

To get down to the nitty-gritty of these sheets, a hotel bed dressed in a percale weave boasts a crisp look and feel, almost as if it were made from your favorite pressed button-down shirt. A sateen weave, however, is polished and resembles the appearance of pearls. What’s more, both of these high-quality sheets have breathable, wrinkle-resistant qualities for a refined aesthetic we know and love in a high-end establishment.

Many of our favorite places to buy bedding—including Italian luxury brands like Frette—even create custom bed linens like these for the best hotels around the world. Scroll below for a staycation-style set of sheets.

For consistency, all of the prices reflect queen sizes. However, many brands offer twin size and king size options too.

The Andersen Hotel, a family-owned boutique retreat in Copenhagen, offers guests sheets, towels, and robes from the editor-favorite brand Boll & Branch. To mimic the experience at home, you can shop the entire collection, including the Signature Hemmed Sheet Set tested and beloved by contributor Rachel Fletcher. The buttery-soft cotton sateen set is made with long-staple cotton fibers, and only gets softer with each wash. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, makes them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” Fletcher shares. After more than five years with these sheets, Fletcher adds that there are no signs of pilling or wear, “just that coveted softness which feels lived-in but not worn out.”

Matouk is a legacy brand known for bespoke touches on high-thread-count sheets. Their hotel collection is found in a number of luxury resorts and historic inns, including Hotel Barrière Fouquet's in New York City and renowned Arizona wellness escape Castle Hot Springs. The Bergamo is their most lightweight percale sheet, combining Giza 87 and 92 Egyptian cotton yarns. “I hate scratchy sheets, and I breathed a sigh of relief when I slipped into these,” says contributor Allie Weiss. “They are lightweight, crisp-looking, and soft to the touch.” We also recommend taking advantage of their personalization feature, which allows you to add a monogram to the edge of the sheet. Just remember that each piece is sold separately, so you’ll have to build your own bedscape.

Another property with Frette bedding, The Palace Hotel in Madrid is an AD-favorite historic hotel. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” As for the bedding, you can mirror the hotel’s lavish interiors with Frette’s bold sheets. The polished sateen set boasts a thick border in six color combinations to wake up a bedroom.

Make a statement without sacrificing a classic hotel look with this tuxedo sheet set. Crafted by Frette for the Ritz-Carlton, this design includes a white-on-white stripe pattern that is perfect for a suite-inspired space. For a unique touch, you can also pair a set of the classic pillowcases with this set for a blend of solid colors and bold lines. Instead of shorter threads that can fray over time, this fabric is made of extra-long staple cotton sateen for an ultra-soft and durable feel.

Priding themselves on a sustainable outlook toward hospitality, the 1 Hotel Group offers a connection with nature and serenity even in the heart of the city. With green-certified buildings and a focus on wellness, it’s no surprise that this hotel’s bedding is equally natural. Kassatex’s 100% cotton sheets are softer than percale but not as shiny as sateen. Contributor Kate McGregor stayed at the 1 Hotel Seattle and was impressed with the breathability. “I’m quite a hot sleeper, but even after a cross-country flight, I slept soundly,” she says. “There was no swishing noise as I moved, either, a pet peeve of mine with really crisp hotel sheets.” Machine washable and available in either a queen or king set, these sheets come with a 60-day trial, so you can really get a feel for them without worrying about a wasted investment.

What Type of Sheets Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

While it varies from property to property, the majority of the hotels on this list use white cotton sheets. Whether percale or sateen, the best hotel sheets all offer a neat, design-agnostic look that suits the center of New York just as well as the rolling hills of Tuscany. Percale will have an added crispness and cooling factor, while sateen will have an added shine and smoothness. Regardless of material finish, look for an all-natural fiber makeup (like 100% cotton) and a versatile white colorway.

Why Do Hotels Like to Use White Bed Sheets?

From an aesthetic perspective, white sheets offer a cloudlike, serene escape for the guest. They also look the cleanest. Stark white sheets cannot hide stains or wear and tear as darker colors can—you can see exactly where each thread has snagged. White bedding is also the most easily sanitized; it even has its own setting on your washing machine. Bleach is necessary to kill germs, especially in a commercial setting, and you don’t want to risk the color fading and yellow stains that can occur on colored sheets.

What Type of Sheets Does The Ritz-Carlton Use?

The Ritz-Carlton uses white cotton sheets from luxury bedding brand Frette. The extra-long staple cotton is more durable than short strands, proven wash after wash. Boasting a subtle monochromatic stripe, The Ritz-Carlton’s sheets play with texture without departing from the clean lines and opulent energy of their suites' overall design scheme.

What Fabrics Are the Best Sheets Made of?

Long or extra-long-staple cotton sheets are considered the “best,” in our experience. These typically have a smooth finish and hold up well over time. That said, so much of it comes down to your own personal preferences. “[Deciding] which one is best for a particular person or climate is relative,” Katie Glusica, professor in the fibers department at the Savannah College of Art and Design, previously shared. “A percale in the 200 to 400 thread-count range will be durable and have a cooler sensation and a lighter weight feel, best for people who run a little warm or where the climate is warmer. Sateen sheets in the 300- to 600-thread-count range are best for someone looking for softness over durability, and better for cooler climates where a heavier feeling sheet is more comfortable.” Then, there are the more seasonal fabrics like airy linen for summer or thick flannel for winter. If you’re still undecided, we often find that Goldilocks-level comfort in cotton sheets with thread counts between 200 and 600 threads per inch.

What Are the Best Bed Sheets for Hot Sleepers and Cold Sleepers?

While percale is recommended for hot or warm sleepers, compared to other cotton sheets, shopping writer Julia Harrison argues the best is bamboo or Tencel lyocell. “AD editors and I prefer these natural fibers because they usually feel cool and gentle against skin, but they also have great temperature regulating qualities since the fabric absorbs excess moisture to help you stay refreshed while you sleep,” she says.

And during the winter months, or for those who run cold year-round, there’s nothing more comforting than sinking into a bed dressed in flannel sheets. “These are great for keeping you cozy and toasty because of a brushed (and sometimes double-brushed) cotton material that feels soft to the touch,” says senior shopping editor Nashia Baker. “It depends on the brand, but some make their sheets with 100% long-staple cotton, like supima cotton, that’s known for its durability without wear over time.”

What Is the Difference Between Percale and Sateen?

Both are made from cotton, but the weave is what differentiates the two. “Percale is a classic one-over, one-under construction that creates a crisp, breathable fabric with a matte finish reminiscent of fine poplin shirting, while sateen’s longer thread float produces a smoother hand and subtle sheen,” Rebecca Weinstein, vice president of design at Highgate, the management company for the Atlas Hotel in Boston, previously told AD. Hot sleepers will feel most comfortable in cooling sheets like percale, while those who prefer a less structured, smooth feel will likely splurge on sateen. “Sateen is more dense, with more threads packed in, so the fabric is warmer,” shared Preeti Gopinath, associate professor of textiles and founding director of the MFA textiles program at Parsons School of Design in New York. “Percale is cooler, and with a thread count of 150 to 200, there is less fabric per square inch, which allows for better airflow.”

#4867. Privacy coins face diverging fortunes as KuCoin moves to drop Monero

KuCoin has already suspended XMR deposits and plans to close withdrawals on Dec. 31. XMR fell 10.5% to $449.98 as of 7:00 p.m. UTC on Thursday. The drop extends a decline from about $625 on Nov. 3.

Launched in 2014, Monero conceals transaction amounts and the wallet addresses of senders and recipients by default. Unlike Monero, Zcash (ZEC), launched in 2016, allows users to choose between transparent and shielded transactions. Both cryptocurrencies have faced regulatory scrutiny over the past few years, with Binance delisting Monero in 2024 and Kraken ending support for it in the European Economic Area later that year.

Zach Pandl, head of research at Grayscale, which launched the first US spot ZEC exchange-traded fund (ETF) in August, said Zcash is positioned differently from Monero. He told Cointelegraph that the firm’s commitment to Zcash will continue for “many years to come.”

Related: Bitwise seeks Texas Stock Exchange listing for Zcash ETF

Pandl said that viewing keys allow Zcash holders to disclose transactions “to an auditor or regulator, law enforcement if they need.” He said the feature gives users greater control over who can access their financial information. “That is exactly how the financial system works today. It’s just that it gives the authority to individuals rather than institutions,” he said.

However, whether viewing keys alone can satisfy regulatory requirements remains a point of debate.

Pandl said that as AI has advanced, it has become “much easier to link pseudonymous addresses with offchain information.” Monero, he explained, uses ring signatures that obscure the source of transactions among multiple possible signers, a method Pandl said “may be vulnerable” as AI-powered blockchain analytics improve.

“We believe strongly that Zcash is the stronger tech,” he said, because “it takes a shielding approach rather than an obfuscation approach.” Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs to verify shielded transactions without publicly revealing sensitive transaction data onchain.

Grayscale’s ETF reached $1 billion in assets under management on Sept. 24, but that figure had fallen to $406 million on Wednesday. Zcash more than tripled in value this year, rising to $1,653 on Sept. 26 from $524 on Jan. 1, according to Token Terminal data. Its price more than doubled in the month following the ETF’s launch but has since fallen back to $770. The cryptocurrency remains up about 50% year to date.

Pandl described Zcash’s price appreciation over the past year as “Bitcoin’s Solana moment,” referring to Solana’s growing market cap and its challenge to Ethereum’s dominance as the “leading smart contract platform.”

“At 1.2% of Bitcoin’s market cap, I would still consider Zcash at a relatively low value,” he said, adding that Grayscale has no price targets for ZEC.

#4865. Kalshi Courts Small Businesses With 'Microinsurance' as State Crackdowns Bite

Kalshi Courts Small Businesses With 'Microinsurance' as State Crackdowns Bite

Prediction market Kalshi is pitching its platform to small businesses as a form of insurance, as legal fights with states over its sports contracts mount.

About 500 businesses have used Kalshi to hedge risks ranging from commodity price swings to extreme weather and power outages, Nicolas Hull, the company's director of business development, told the Financial Times. Hull described the offering as "almost a form of microinsurance," but said almost all of the small businesses he had spoken to had never hedged before.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

One New York rice brand plans to pay about $9,000 for contracts that would pay out up to $60,000 if new tariffs on Indian rice imports hit, according to the FT. A new crop of brokers is using AI tools to find small businesses exposed to regulatory changes, such as tariffs or tax increases, and structure contracts for them to trade.

Event organizers have used the same approach. NEXTPredict, which runs a prediction markets conference, paid a $12,000 premium for Kalshi contracts that would have returned about $3 million if more than half of scheduled arrivals at New York's JFK airport were cancelled the day before its October event, with trading firm Susquehanna taking the other side. The conference went ahead as planned, so the contracts did not pay out.

It is not Kalshi's first attempt to move beyond retail betting. It has also struck a deal with Game Point Capital to enter the sports insurance market.

The business markets are still small. Kalshi is offering cash incentives to traders to provide enough liquidity for businesses to take part, according to the FT, and insurance broker Lockton told the newspaper it had not yet seen much uptake. Kalshi also turned down a request to hedge wildfire risk, citing its policy against markets that could create "perverse incentives" for traders, the FT reported.

Sports have dominated Kalshi's trading. About 87% of the $39.7 billion traded on the platform in the year to February 2026 was on sports, according to a Congressional Research Service report, and Kentucky has alleged that sports made up 89% of its 2025 volume.

Kalshi's diversification push comes amid an escalation in its legal fights this week. The prediction market paused operations in the state on Monday after failing to persuade a federal appeals court to halt Utah's enforcement actions, spokesperson Jacki McGavick told Ars Technica, cutting off what she said were more than 177,000 users.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown's office then moved to dismiss the 14 criminal charges it filed in October against Kalshi and its co-founders, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara, after Kalshi agreed to block users in the state, the office said. The dismissal is without prejudice, meaning the charges can be refiled. Including Kalshi, seven prediction market companies have agreed to stop operating in Utah.

Kalshi has stopped taking bets from Utahns. Utah law treats betting on sports and other events as gambling, and that includes prediction markets. The Office is moving to dismiss its 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and individual defendants, and may refile them if Kalshi takes… pic.twitter.com/vjLJpoynaO

— Office of the Utah Attorney General (@UtahAG) November 24, 2026

"Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges," Brown said. Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth tweeted that "good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized."

Elsewhere, Arkansas has sued Kalshi, and New York's attorney general is seeking $3.6 billion from the company. On Monday, a New York judge denied the state's request for a temporary restraining order that risked shutting Kalshi down nationwide, and urged it to limit bets by users under 21, Scripps News reported. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has invoked emergency powers to keep Kalshi trading there.

Kalshi expects the question of who regulates prediction markets to reach the Supreme Court. So far, three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate the platforms, and one has found they cannot. Meanwhile, the CFTC has set out new rules to separate prediction markets from gambling, and the Senate has passed a bill banning bets on war, terrorism and death.

#4864. 'I Kickstarted My Upper-Body Strength Transformation Using Only A 25-Lb. Bag Of Rice'

"I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life."

As soon as I started walking, I was playing a sport. I don’t remember there being a time where I wasn't on a sports team during my childhood. To me, exercise was practice after school and traveling for games on the weekend for whatever sport I was playing. As a teen, in my off-seasons, my mom would beg me to go to the gym with her for fun, but I didn't have much interest in it.

I liked running and endurance-based activities because I felt like they complimented sports pretty well, especially lacrosse, which eventually became my main activity. I ended up being able to play lacrosse in college, where I was first required to start strength training to prepare for the season. While I was in shape for my sport, I couldn’t even lift the bar in the gym, and I was mesmerized by all the different movements that I didn’t really understand.

In the middle of college, everyone was sent home because of the pandemic. I felt far away from my entire life and all my friends, and like there was nothing for me to be doing. There was so much time on my hands, and there was nowhere for me to be.

While sitting at home alone, I had nothing to do besides work out. To pass the time and cope with what was happening, I wanted to exercise, but I felt stuck since gyms were closed.

Then my dad handed me this 25-pound bag of rice from Costco and said, “You can train with this. There’s actually a lot you can do with it.” So I stuffed that bag of rice in a backpack to make it heavy, and I’d use it as a weight. I would put the backpack at the front of my body and do squats. I would use it as a kettlebell for kettlebell swings. I would put it on my back and do walking lunges.

I realized there was a lot I could do at home, but I wanted to try to strength train at the actual gym. I decided that, when I was done playing college lacrosse, I would get serious about a gym routine.

When I graduated from college, I was excited—but so confused—about where to begin. I followed fitness influencers on TikTok who gave workout tips and advice on which movements to try. But I also wanted to make sure all of my information was accurate and science-based, so I started researching online, watching the moves other people at the gym were doing, and reaching out to my old college coaches for tips.

At first, I thought I needed to be running and lifting every day to stay fit, but I soon realized I was over-exerting my body. I started learning more about the basics of strength training and how to work different muscles with compound movements like squats, deadlifts, hang cleans, and more. I also learned how to supplement those movements by doing auxiliary exercises with dumbbells or body weight exercises like curls, lunges, and more.

After a combination of trial and error, researching, and practicing at the gym, I finally found my strength training routine and stride. I started to finally perfect my strength exercises. My confidence was growing so much as a result, which only motivated me to continue. I developed so much discipline that translated into every other aspect of my life.

Even when things got off-routine for me, I could fall back into strength training to find my rhythm again. I know it’ll always be there, giving me structure even when everything else feels unsettled.

When I first started lifting, I was hungrier because I was training more, but I was afraid to eat more. But if you want to build muscle, you need protein and you have to eat! It’s how your body survives and thrives. You need to take care of yourself, and that includes getting enough sleep.

I do not always feel motivated to workout. That’s just how life is. But when I started strength training, I developed so much discipline. Even when I don’t have motivation, that discipline is there now, not just at the gym. Stick with it and allow that habit to form.

It’s honestly true when they say that movement is medicine. When I'm taking care of my body, even if my mental headspace isn't in peak condition, I feel better after movement. It’s not all about hitting personal bests, either. (Though those certainly help!) I might tell myself, “I don't want to go to the gym today, but I will because I know it’s good for me.” Strength training gives me the confidence to know I can do anything I set my mind to.

Nowadays, I strength train four days a week, and I’ll also do a designated cardio day. I base my training on muscle groups.

Each workout will have a main exercise, such as a squat, bench press, or deadlift. Then, I pair them with auxiliary exercises like lunges, quad extensions, hamstring curls, rear delt flies, incline dumbbell bench presses, and more that target smaller muscles.

I try to stay between four to five exercises per workout so I don't overdo it. I like to keep it simple when I write my workout plans. I’ll follow those plans for a certain number of weeks depending on my goals, then I’ll move on from there. I like to keep things interesting for myself to ensure I never get bored, because I want to be able to do this forever.

I used to not be able to hang clean the bar, and once I even dropped it on my knee and ruptured my bursa. It was all bruised, and I was so embarrassed. From then on, I had a real mental block with hang cleans. I told myself, “I’m never going to be able to do a lot of weight.”

Years later, I decided it was about time I face my fear. I worked my way up to being able to put 25-pound plates on each side, coming out to about 100 pounds, depending on the bar. The more I practiced, the easier it became for me, and getting there was a huge milestone.

Any upper-body movements are especially empowering to me. Many people don’t think you can have impressive upper-body strength as a woman. When I was able to work my way up to putting a 45-pound weight on each side for bench presses, coming out to 135 pounds, I felt unstoppable. It was such a big deal to me since I never thought I’d be able to do it. It’s such an empowering feeling to be doing something that a lot of people see as something only men would do.

#4862. AI is driving a flood of crypto bug reports. Now it’s helping sort them

Bug bounty platform HackerOne said it’s increasing its triage throughput with AI agents after a record quarter of reports in the third quarter.

Crypto bug bounty platforms have expanded their use of artificial intelligence to keep up with a growing mountain of AI-assisted security reports.

Crypto-focused HackenProof said in October that it was using AI to triage 70% of submissions fully autonomously, aiming to hit 85% by the end of 2026. It said it received an average of about 6,100 bug reports a month in the third quarter, 2.4 times the reports from December last year.

Rival Immunefi last week said submissions to its platform rose 136% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, as it introduced a tool that can flag duplicates before a researcher submits a report.

Bug bounty programs pay independent researchers to find and report potential security flaws. AI has helped researchers uncover more genuine vulnerabilities, but has also swelled the volume of invalid and duplicate submissions, making it harder for security teams to identify the threats that need urgent attention.

It’s like “bringing a sword to a gunfight,” Dmitry Tokarev, founder of crypto wallet provider Bron, told Cointelegraph, referring to security teams that haven’t already adopted AI to sift through reports.

Several bug bounty platforms have identified February as a turning point in the surge of AI-assisted vulnerability reports, coinciding with the release of more capable AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6.

HackenProof said Claude Opus 4.6 could work through larger codebases and sustain tasks for longer. HackerOne said the arrival of more capable AI models and tools in that month saw a sudden shift from a “human-only submission environment.”

Graph showing HackenProof's volume of bug reports per month. Source: HackenProof

Some crypto developers are also experimenting with financial disincentives to curb low-quality submissions.

The team behind Firedancer, a Solana validator client developed by Jump Crypto, which also uses AI to screen reports, took an additional measure in October.

To deter spam, it began requiring researchers to burn 1 SOL for each bug report they want considered for a bounty. The token is permanently destroyed, even if the report turns out to be a duplicate.

In a November update published Tuesday, HackerOne’s vice president of operations Tony Lee said they began requiring researchers to verify their identities before submitting reports in the third quarter. It also expanded its triage team and began using AI agents to automatically close clear-cut cases, such as spam and duplicate reports.

In October, it gave customers more control over how many reports their public programs receive.

Related: AI labs likely sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells,’ computer scientist says

Lee said he expects vulnerability reports to keep climbing “for the foreseeable future” after recording a 22% increase in report volume in Q3 compared to the previous quarter.

Meanwhile, insurer QBE and risk consultancy Control Risks on Wednesday forecast more disruptive cyber incidents in 2027 across the 14 markets they studied, pointing to the “industrialization of AI” as one of the factors.

Mike Blank, chief product officer at blockchain infrastructure firm R3, also said he expects the number of hacks to rise sharply in 2027, but said crypto teams should pay closer attention to how much damage a single breach can cause, rather than the number of attacks.

“The real difference will be between protocols where a stolen key can drain everything and those where it can only pause operations,” Blank said.

On Khalil’s days off, he cooks breakfast. The boys eat at a round dining table with a shattered-glass finish, leather bar stools in cognac around it. But when morning light fills the room, Brianna takes it in. “This is beautiful,” she says. “This is our space.”

“He loves his wife—I mean, he’s obsessed with her—and he loves his kids. I’ve never seen a guy like that,” Ryan Saghian says. Brianna Mack with Deuce and Kylo in the primary suite’s sitting area. Sofa by J.Alexander Furniture; artwork by William McLure; Moroccan alpaca-mohair rug from Caravan Rugs.

The primary suite’s sitting area. Sofa by J.Alexander Furniture in S.Harris fabric; swivel chairs and coffee table by Eichholtz Los Angeles; pendant by Vakkerlight in alabaster and saddle leather; Moroccan alpaca-mohair rug from Caravan Rugs; artwork by William McLure; florals by Goodroots LA.

“This is a guy who comes home exhausted not only mentally but physically,” Saghian says of Khalil. So they knocked down walls and rebuilt what was necessary: hyperbaric chamber, massage space. “I needed a spot like this to just relax and recover,” Khalil says. Brianna took a room nearby for hair and makeup. And when the work is done, there’s a screening room that includes a pit-style sofa, a candy bar, and a glowing fiber-optic ceiling. Saghian borrowed the last detail from a Rolls-Royce. “I look at [game] film in there if I need to,” Khalil says. “But it’s more fun to watch movies as a family there.”

A black marble soaking tub, so heavy it required building approval before it could enter the elevator, sits between dual rain showers. Checkerboard floor in black and cream marble.

In the boy’s bedroom, the bed wall is entirely custom, with twin beds set into niches and recessed shelves; footballs from their father line the opposite wall. Bedding by Parachute; chest by Pottery Barn; rug by Nordik Knots.

“We really own this space,” Brianna says. “A place for our boys to feel loved and to have a sense of identity.” She had hoped for something good. A life they built from the studs up.

#4860. Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension Four Weeks After $6.4B Hack

Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension Four Weeks After $6.4B Hack

Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it imposed after the record $6.4 billion hack of the exchange in October, four weeks after the attack.

"Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted," the exchange said in an announcement on Thursday.

Service Recovery Update:Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted. Withdrawals are open across nearly all networks. Separately, a small number are temporarily paused due to network maintenance, which… pic.twitter.com/QZmXhsc2qA

Withdrawals for a small number of networks are still temporarily paused while they undergo maintenance or planned upgrades, affecting a very small percentage of regular traffic, Binance said. That is separate from its recovery work and part of its standard practice of pausing a network's withdrawals when external conditions require it, the exchange added.

Binance said all user assets remain fully backed, and pointed users to its proof of reserves website, where they can check that their holdings are backed at least 1:1.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BNB with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The exchange also warned that events like the hack can attract phishing attempts. It said it will never ask users for their passwords, two-factor authentication codes or seed phrases, and will never contact them to "speed up withdrawals," offer "priority processing," or move their assets into a "Binance vault."

The FBI has attributed the October 29 attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. North Korea has denied involvement. Binance set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses after the hack, and has won a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts.

Efforts to recover the stolen crypto are ongoing. On Monday, the U.S. Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture action for more than $1.1 billion in USDC stolen in the hack, and said the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto since the attack.

The hackers have continued to move what they still control. More than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through cross-chain exchange THORChain, according to estimates from blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and Elliptic, Reuters reported. Elliptic told the news agency that $342 million has also moved through a Bitcoin coinjoin service, a technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, up from the $247 million it reported earlier this week.

Laundering the funds could take months or even years, but cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea, TRM Labs' global head of policy Ari Redbord told Reuters.

The FBI on October 31 called on crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block addresses linked to the hack. THORChain, which says it does not censor transactions or carry out Know Your Customer checks, may have earned as much as $1 million in fees from the launderers' swaps, according to TRM Labs estimates cited by Reuters.

Why not just shut THORChain down after a hack?@CBarraford's answer to @RBoccius : by his count, 98% of THORChain's volume is legitimate trading. Shut it down and you hit all those people, the ones using it for their own financial freedom.

The hackers would barely notice.… pic.twitter.com/ax7Bwz9Uvu

— THORChain (@THORChain) November 26, 2026

THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford defended the protocol in a video posted by THORChain on Thursday, saying that by his count 98% of its volume is legitimate trading. Shutting it down would hurt those who use the system for "completely neutral and good purposes for their own individual financial freedom and liberty," while barely inconveniencing the hackers, he argued. Bad actors will "find a way to get out just the same, they'll still go through Russian dark net things or Chinese," he said.

#4858. Ethereum devs set Glamsterdam’s Hoodi rollout for mid-December after delays

Glamsterdam’s Hoodi upgrade was delayed in October after concerns that changes to gas pricing could break some existing smart contracts.

Ethereum core developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade for the Hoodi testnet on Dec. 15, nearly two months after it was originally due to go live.

Among a number of upgrades, Glamsterdam changes how much gas Ethereum charges for certain operations under two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. However, testing found that under the new rules, some smart contracts could run out of gas and fail, prompting developers to delay the Hoodi rollout originally set for Oct. 26.

In an All Core Developers Consensus call on Thursday, Ethereum developers set Dec. 15 for Glamsterdam’s activation on the Hoodi testnet. Execution-layer teams reached broad agreement to keep EIP-8037 as written after some developers warned that revising the gas pricing proposal could break other smart contracts and further delay the mainnet rollout.

Ethereum researcher and core developer Ansgar Dietrichs said leaving the question open would have pushed the Hoodi rollout into 2027. “Indecision is also just a decision in itself; it would just mean we delay into the next year,” he said.

Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade made it to the Sepolia testnet on Oct. 6, while Hoodi is the final testnet before it goes to mainnet.

The upgrade aims to advance Ethereum’s layer-1 scaling roadmap with enshrined proposer-builder separation, block-level access lists and changes to gas pricing that better reflect the cost of execution.

Last week, Ethereum Foundation’s Rahul Kothari said mid-January would be the earliest viable date for a mainnet rollout, and that the three projects with the highest-severity compatibility issues had either applied fixes or expected to do so by mid-December.

Some projects with medium-severity issues had given timelines as late as Jan. 10.

#4855. This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Sánchez added a new architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” says Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

The first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a new floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

In the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

The primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

#4854. Japan’s crypto security group taps SEAL to speed up hack response

The partnership comes weeks after a third-party data breach exposed hundreds of thousands of customer email addresses belonging to two Japanese crypto exchanges.

Japan’s crypto industry cybersecurity group has signed an agreement with US nonprofit Security Alliance (SEAL) to improve the detection of cyberattacks and respond to incidents more effectively.

According to a statement released Friday, the memorandum will see JPCrypto-ISAC receive help from SEAL to develop an incident response support framework and give them access to SEAL’s incident response and support capabilities. Both organizations will also share cyber threat intelligence.

In the Web3 and digital asset sector, addressing cyber threats that transcend national borders has become essential, said JPCrypto-ISAC representative director Naoji Noda. “We are delighted to establish this partnership with SEAL through this MOU.”

JPCrypto-ISAC had 16 full members at launch in 2025, including SBI VC Trade, bitbank, GMO Coin and Rakuten Wallet. The organization helps Japanese crypto companies share and analyze cyber threat intelligence.

Earlier this month, Japanese crypto exchanges Zaif and CoinTrade disclosed that a breach at their email provider, Arara, exposed hundreds of thousands of customer email addresses.

Arara estimated that the breach may have affected up to 380 companies across its customer base.

Japan’s crypto industry suffered a major breach in May 2024, when hackers stole Bitcoin worth about $305 million at the time from crypto exchange DMM Bitcoin. US and Japanese authorities later attributed the theft to North Korean hackers.

#4852. What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond

What's on the Ethereum Roadmap: Glamsterdam, Hegotá and Beyond

Like all blockchain projects, Ethereum is under active development, with upgrades designed to make it faster, cheaper, and easier to use.

Instead of a single "Ethereum 2.0" event, the network upgrades through coordinated changes called hard forks that introduce new features or modify how the protocol operates.

Since the Merge in September 2022, developers have focused on scaling, lowering transaction costs, improving wallets, and making it easier to run nodes and validators. The Ethereum community is also aiming for roughly two major upgrades per year when research and testing are ready.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Ethereum's scaling plan relies on layer-2 networks. These are separate blockchains built on top of Ethereum that process transactions off-chain and send results back to Ethereum for security and settlement.

Many layer-2 systems use rollups, which bundle multiple transactions together and post them to Ethereum as a single batch, allowing Ethereum to support more activity without the base chain processing every transaction.

As a result, much of Ethereum's development has focused on making it cheaper and easier for rollups to use the network. More recent upgrades have also aimed to scale Ethereum's base layer directly, by raising the amount of activity each block can hold.

In July 2022, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin described the network's six roadmap phases as the Merge, the Surge, the Scourge, the Verge, the Purge, and the Splurge.

These phases are not single upgrades but broad goals, and several progress in parallel.

Ethereum's roadmap is implemented through a series of hard forks.

Glamsterdam is the upgrade after Fusaka, and its name combines "Amsterdam," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devconnect location, and "Gloas," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star. It focuses on scaling Ethereum's base layer, with two headline features:

Glamsterdam also raises the gas cost of creating new state, such as accounts and contracts, to target database growth of about 120 GiB a year, and reprices reading stored data, to keep hardware requirements manageable as capacity rises. Under one proposal, EIP-8037, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as before.

Other scheduled changes would make a standard ETH transfer between existing accounts up to 71% cheaper, let developers deploy contracts to the same address across chains, make ETH transfers emit a log that apps can track, raise the maximum contract size from about 24KiB to 64KiB, and speed up validator exits and consolidations.

Node operators and stakers will need to update their clients to support the fork; ETH holders do not need to do anything.

Developers originally targeted the first half of 2026. Glamsterdam went live on the Sepolia testnet in October 2026, but a fork on the Hoodi testnet planned for October 26, 2026, was postponed after security firm ChainSecurity warned that the upgrade's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existing smart contracts.

In November 2026, developers rescheduled the Hoodi fork for December 15, 2026, and agreed to ship the gas changes unaltered. As of November 2026, no mainnet date had been set.

Hegotá is the upgrade planned to follow Glamsterdam. Its name combines "Bogotá," the execution layer upgrade named after a previous Devcon location, and "Heze," the consensus layer upgrade named after a star.

As of its October 2026 update, ethereum.org expected Hegotá on mainnet in the second quarter of 2027, with a fork on the Sepolia testnet to come first, though no dates had been confirmed. Two changes are scheduled for inclusion.

The headliner, Fork-choice Enforced Inclusion Lists (FOCIL, EIP-7805), aims to strengthen censorship resistance by having a committee of validators propose lists of transactions that block builders must include, so that no single party can keep a valid transaction out of a block. Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would let each account set its own rules for what counts as a valid transaction, rather than relying on a single fixed signature scheme. That would bring features such as social recovery, spending limits, multiple approvals and gas sponsorship directly into the protocol, and let accounts adopt signature schemes designed to resist quantum computers.

Dozens of other proposals are being considered, but none are settled, and the rest of Hegotá's scope is still being decided. In November 2026, some developers argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, with a decision on Hegotá's full scope expected in December 2026. Forkcast tracks the live status of each proposal.

Upgrade names and scopes can change during development as proposals are refined before each hard fork.

Ethereum's roadmap continues to evolve as research progresses and upgrades are tested on devnets and testnets before mainnet deployment.

This article was updated in November 2026, and will be amended as as new milestones are confirmed.

#4851. New York AG secures $1.37B court judgment against NovaTech founders

The judgment follows an August 2025 default ruling against the founders over a Ponzi scheme that targeted Haitian and other immigrant communities.

New York Attorney General Letitia James secured a $1.367 billion court judgment against Cynthia and Eddy Petion, the founders of defunct crypto and forex trading company NovaTech, over an investment scheme that defrauded hundreds of thousands of people.

“Today’s historic judgment finally delivers some semblance of justice for the thousands of New Yorkers who were targeted by this merciless scam,” James said in a Wednesday press release.

In October, James sought a court order for the Petions and affiliated companies to pay about $1.37 billion, including $1.13 billion in investor funds and $232.5 million in interest. The request followed a default judgment issued in August 2025, which found the company and its founders liable by default after the couple fled the country and failed to respond to the lawsuit.

James sued NovaTech in June 2024, alleging that the platform targeted immigrant communities, particularly Haitian New Yorkers, through prayer groups and social media, promising high returns on investments. Over 11,000 New Yorkers lost tens of millions of dollars to NovaTech and an earlier crypto mining scheme, AWS Mining.

AWS Mining collapsed in 2019, while NovaTech followed suit in 2023.

#4850. This Designer Finds Unexpected Beauty in Marble’s Leftovers

Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the New York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak says.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” says the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”

#4848. AI-Powered GTA 6 PC Ports Now Have Multiplayer as Modders Unlock 30 and 60 FPS

AI-Powered GTA 6 PC Ports Now Have Multiplayer as Modders Unlock 30 and 60 FPS

Gamers managed to get multiplayer working on GTA 6 for PC before Rockstar Games managed to release GTA 6 for PC. And they're apparently making the console version run better than the original, too.

A developer going by TeK shared footage Thursday showing multiple players interacting within the same game world in an unofficial PC build of Grand Theft Auto 6. The implementation reportedly supports character and vehicle synchronization, as well as proximity voice chat, running at between 25 and 30 frames per second (FPS).

GTA VI Working Multiplayer, Character, Vehicles & Proximity voice chat. (25-30FPS)#GTAVI #GTA6 pic.twitter.com/PyWvg764zZ

The development comes just a day after Decrypt reported that some AI-assisted ports were struggling to achieve 20 FPS while consuming upwards of 40 GB of system memory.

Another development team, known as BoYoo, demonstrated gameplay averaging 27 FPS during a boat mission, using an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, an Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, and 32 GB of RAM. Memory consumption dropped to approximately 15.4 GB, although performance in the more demanding downtown areas of Vice City remains untested.

No son 60 FPS en el GTA de los Mares del SUR en PS5 pero NADA MAL CHAVALES!! pic.twitter.com/L63ALb7JAu

— NanospeedGamer (@NanospeedGamer) November 26, 2026

Developers have also demonstrated in-game modification menus, allowing them to manipulate elements of the game for debugging purposes.

Meanwhile, console modders have released a patch that removes GTA 6's 30 FPS cap on jailbroken PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles. The latter reportedly exceeds 50 FPS during gameplay without relying on AI-generated intermediate frames.

The patch doesn't guarantee a consistent 60 FPS, but it does offer the potential for smoother gameplay and more responsive controls than Rockstar's officially supported version. For some players, modifying their console could arguably provide a better gameplay experience.

The advancements come despite Rockstar's parent company, Take-Two Interactive, successfully taking down 3,007 GitHub repositories associated with Project Leonida, one of the most prominent efforts to bring the game to PC using AI coding tools.

Developers are using AI to reverse-engineer a leaked Xbox build of the game and adapt its code to run on computers, dramatically accelerating a process that traditionally required extensive manual work.

Rockstar has historically made PC gamers wait. Grand Theft Auto 5 arrived on PC in April 2015, roughly 19 months after its original console release, while Red Dead Redemption 2 took just over a year.

Generative AI could make that business strategy considerably riskier.

Obbe Vermeij, a former technical director at Rockstar North, warned about precisely this scenario before GTA 6's release.

“I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC,” Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun in an interview.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short NVDA with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Vermeij estimated that such an undertaking could cost tens of thousands of dollars in AI processing. Even if the resulting product fell short of Rockstar's official version, he suggested it could be good enough to satisfy some PC gamers, giving the company an incentive to bring its release dates closer together.

Wall Street has been paying attention, too.

During Take-Two's November 9 earnings call, Raymond James analyst Andrew Marok asked management how AI-assisted reverse engineering and decompilation were affecting the company's approach to security and development.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick acknowledged that piracy would become more challenging, although he maintained that replicating the intended experience of its games would remain technically difficult.

“I think it will be manageable, and we are focused on it,” Zelnick said.

There is some academic research suggesting that early piracy can substantially affect video game sales. A 2024 study published in Entertainment Computing by researcher William Volckmann examined games protected by Denuvo, an anti-piracy technology, and estimated average revenue losses of 20% when that protection was broken particularly early in a game's commercial life.

That figure cannot be directly extrapolated to GTA 6, which has yet to enter the PC market. But a sufficiently polished unofficial port distributed for free months before Rockstar's commercial release could reduce the number of players willing to pay full price for the same story they have already completed.

Rockstar would still have advantages, including official multiplayer servers, technical support, downloadable content, and a more polished gaming experience. The unofficial multiplayer implementation remains far removed from the scale of GTA Online, and none of the community projects has independently demonstrated that the entire campaign can be completed reliably.

GTA 6 generated an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day alone, according to a regulatory filing by Take-Two. Twenty percent of that would amount to roughly $758 million in lost sales revenue.

Rockstar still hasn't announced a PC release date.

#4847. ESMA to overhaul EU’s MiCA crypto register in 2027

ESMA’s new MiCA register will replace manual reporting and introduce automated data checks and a version history for crypto white papers.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is preparing an overhaul of its public crypto register nearly two years after its launch.

The European Union’s securities watchdog plans to replace its manual interim register under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) with a searchable web-based platform around mid-2027, an ESMA spokesperson told Cointelegraph.

The new system will also maintain a version history for individual white papers to provide archives of changes.

MiCA’s transitional period ended in July, which meant that unauthorized crypto service providers had to wind down their EU operations or face multimillion-euro fines or other enforcement action. ESMA’s interim register serves as a public reference point for checking whether a crypto company is authorized in the bloc.

ESMA launched its interim register in December 2024, publishing downloadable spreadsheet files containing information supplied by national regulators.

“The new IT system will replace the current manual email-based submission and consolidation process with a structured web-based interface through which national competent authorities can provide and update information for their relevant entities/white papers,” ESMA said.

The system will also be able to cross-check information against reference databases, including the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF) registry, which maintains a global database of legal entity identifiers.

For white papers, the system will perform technical checks against ESMA’s standardized reporting framework, helping identify missing mandatory information and documents that do not meet formatting requirements.

Another major change concerns how investors access crypto white papers, which outline information about crypto assets, their issuers and associated risks.

“The future register will not rely solely on links to white papers hosted on an entity’s website as is currently the case with the interim solution,” the ESMA spokesperson said, adding: “In the new IT solution, the white papers will be available directly on the register platform.”

Related: Spain moves to grant financial watchdog power to freeze crypto accounts

Users will also be able to download register data in CSV format or retrieve it through application programming interfaces (APIs), although ESMA said it could not yet disclose the full range of planned features.
